articles.title: How bartaco’s Viral ‘CEO Hotline’ Revealed What Guests Actually Want
articles.titleKo: How bartaco’s Viral ‘CEO Hotline’ Revealed What Guests Actually Want
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . We’re living in a time when it’s more likely you’ll talk to an AI chatbot than a human when trying to reach a business. Yet, people are still yelling “speak to operator” into their smart phones, and viral videos show drive-thru customers deliberately trying to confuse AI-voice ordering tech so they can talk to a real person. In what feels like the antithesis to an increasingly AI-saturated world, Anthony Valletta decided to listen to guests (literally) through an unconventional initiative: a “CEO Hotline” that routes diners straight to his personal cell phone. He put his cell number and email address on every guest receipt across all 31 bartaco locations. The receipt says: “If you had a great time, tell a friend. If you didn’t, contact our CEO.” It even adds: “No, this is not a joke.” Since rolling it out, Valletta has been personally taking guest calls, texts, voicemails, and emails every single day, and personally responding to them himself. Some are complaints, some are compliments, and some turn into personal conversations about guests’ experiences with the brand. After a podcast clip about him printing his contact information on every receipt went viral—racking up about 1.6 million views on Instagram and TikTok—Valletta’s CEO hotline exploded. He now spends 45 minutes to two hours a day fielding guest outreach, with weekends bringing as many as 50 to 100 contacts in a single Friday or Saturday. He estimates roughly 80 percent of those messages are compliments or stories guests want to share. “I expected to be dealing mostly with [mostly] guest complaints, and the adverse actually happened,” Valletta adds. “Every piece of feedback to me is so valuable that it doesn’t matter how big or small. It’s been super insightful.” While many restaurant brands offer generic “contact us” forms, bartaco isn’t aware of another national restaurant chain that goes as far as printing its CEO’s personal contact information on every single guest receipt and actively encouraging guests to reach out. Then, Valletta and his team chose to take it one step further by turning it into a live guest experience on June 2. A blue analog phone was installed at bartaco Port Chester—one of the brand’s oldest and busiest restaurants—where guests could pick up the phone that day and call Valletta live from the restaurant to share feedback, ask questions, talk about their experience, or simply say hello. “We wanted to get that retro nostalgia feeling … The old-school way, where it wasn’t AI enabled, it wasn’t some bot replying,” Valletta says. “Let’s get a retro phone in the restaurant, hooked up to landline, as old school as it goes, and really establish that connectivity, and that’s kind of where the idea came from. It was fun. We were active the whole time, the phone was nonstop, which is pretty cool.” One of the most memorable calls came from a young kid who talked about how much he loves bartaco quesadillas, cheese sticks, and the coloring books, while his mom chimed in from the background to tell him about everything their family loves about the brand. For Valletta, it was validation that bartaco’s intentionally designed kids’ experience is truly resonating with families. But the most eye-opening learning for Valletta, based on a common theme heard across many calls, was that bartaco needed to up its storytelling game. “People were calling, asking questions about things they could actually experience in a restaurant, or things that were coming up from a marketing perspective that hadn’t landed to that guest yet,” he says. Valletta realized that if guests cared enough to pick up the phone and call him, they were clearly passionate about the brand; yet their questions made it clear the company had work to do on clearly communicating existing menu items, returning favorites, and upcoming events. articles.title: Chicago’s Smyth Appoints Conor Dalton as Head Chef
articles.titleKo: Chicago’s Smyth Appoints Conor Dalton as Head Chef
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Smyth, Chicago’s three-MICHELIN-starred fine-dining beacon and 50 Best’s No. 1 Restaurant in North America, has appointed MICHELIN-starred Chef Conor Dalton as Head Chef following a rigorous global search for the world’s rising culinary talent. Building upon a landmark decade of culinary excellence, Smyth is breaking ground on an ambitious new era. Head Chef Conor Dalton will work alongside Executive Chef John Shields and Executive Pastry Chef Karen Urie Shields to uphold Smyth’s rigorous standards while continuously pushing the boundaries of modern gastronomy. Conor Dalton’s appointment marks a bold new epoch for the restaurant, building upon Smyth’s storied legacy as the team charts its next chapter. With over twenty years of experience across internationally renowned fine-dining restaurants, Conor Dalton is well-equipped for this latest venture. Serving as the Head Chef for Skof, Tom Barnes’ Manchester restaurant which achieved a MICHELIN star within only eight months of opening, he has been recognized as an exceptional culinary talent across the United Kingdom and beyond. He has earned a host of accolades, including placement on the National Restaurant Awards 2025’s Chef to Watch Shortlist, an honor bestowed upon only the best of the best in the culinary industry. Before Skof, Conor Dalton honed his craft in the kitchens of Simon Rogan’s three-MICHELIN-starred L’Enclume and The Five Fields in London, refining his fine-dining techniques and leadership expertise. Now, he eyes his next frontier, signing on as the Head Chef of Smyth, closing out a landmark year for the restaurant and breaking ground on its new stage as a gastronomical trailblazer. “Joining this team is a tremendous honor and profound responsibility,” says Head Chef Conor Dalton. “Chefs John and Karen have built one of the world’s most extraordinary dining destinations. I look forward to working alongside them, bringing my own perspective to the kitchen, and contributing to the restaurant’s next chapter of innovation. I’ve always admired the warmth of American hospitality, and to be a part of a restaurant which prioritizes this artistry is a lifelong dream.” Conor Dalton’s appointment comes after an international search by Smyth, seeking out visionary chefs from across the globe to anchor the celebrated restaurant’s high-caliber kitchen. The team was drawn to his discipline, commitment to peak-season produce and collaborative leadership style. John Shields and Conor Dalton initially connected over a conversation surrounding influences, ambitions and an adoration for an intangible, yet all-consuming, sense of hospitality. As part of the selection process for the position, the two chefs met in person, and worked together to pilot this new vision for Smyth’s next chapter. After two days of seamless hands-on collaboration in the kitchen, Conor Dalton emerged as the ideal candidate. “We are thrilled to welcome Chef Conor to our team,” says Executive Chef John Shields. “It is rare to find someone with the raw talent to achieve the excellence we strive for at Smyth. This appointment marks the start of an exciting era as we constantly seek to refine and perfect our craft”. This appointment marks an already historic year for Smyth, earning the title of No. 1 Best Restaurant in North America by 50 Best in May and celebrating its 10 year anniversary earlier this summer. In addition to this year’s achievements, the concept has also earned and retained a third MICHELIN-star in 2023, 2024, and 2025 – the guidebook’s highest and most coveted recognition. Reserve Smyth’s experience at www.smythchicago.com. Smyth is located at 177 North Ada Street in Chicago. For more information on the restaurant, diners can follow its social media at @smythchicago on Facebook and Instagram. articles.title: How Disconnected Systems Slow Down Restaurant Teams
articles.titleKo: How Disconnected Systems Slow Down Restaurant Teams
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . The ability to quickly transfer and unify data and reduce the need for constant switching is mandatory in the modern technology stack. To the average consumer, a restaurant’s success may appear to hinge on one simple factor: the quality of its food. In practice, the success of a restaurant is driven by a much broader set of variables, including staffing, process design, and increasingly, technology infrastructure, all of course in addition to food quality. Today’s restaurant operators rely on an expanding ecosystem of digital tools to manage everything from online ordering and loyalty programs to guest communications and financial reporting. It’s reasonable to think that this shift occurred as a result of the pandemic, but even prior, adoption was quite widespread. Looking to Toast’s 2019 Restaurant Success Report, a mere 3 percent of restaurants reported to have operated without technology vendors. In the seven years since, digital tools have become even more central to day-to-day operations, largely though the form of POS Systems and Online Ordering at the bare minimum. Looking outward, the restaurant technology space has begun a wave of M&A, with brands (take DoorDash for example) purchasing smaller solutions to build a larger unified platform. While partnerships display a commitment to interoperability and the flexibility of a platform to their customer’s custom stack, unified platforms have begun to grow in appeal. While individual solutions often deliver measurable value, a growing challenge has emerged: fragmentation across multiple systems. As operators deploy three, five, or even more platforms to support their business, they introduce complexity that can offset the efficiency gains those tools promise. This has come to take on the name “toggle tax”, capturing the time and cognitive cost associated with switching between applications, re-entering data, and manually reconciling information across systems. A study on the US hospitality industry by Access Hospitality and Paytronix found that 46 percent of restaurant businesses use between two and four systems across their entire suite, with 36 percent of respondents managing at least five systems to run their business. In restaurant environments, where speed and real-time decision-making directly impact revenue, the consequences can be even more pronounced. Fragmented systems can delay access to critical data, reduce staff productivity, and increase the likelihood of errors, particularly when teams must manually bridge gaps between tools. Industry trends suggest this complexity is widespread. Operators today are often managing multiple systems across POS, ordering, loyalty, scheduling, and analytics platforms. When these systems do not integrate effectively, employees spend valuable time navigating between dashboards instead of focusing on guest experience or revenue-generating activities. In some hospitality segments, disconnected systems have been shown to result in significant time losses and operational inefficiencies, ultimately affecting profitability. The impact extends beyond lost time. Context switching research indicates that frequent task switching can reduce productivity by as much as 40 percent and significantly impair decision quality. For restaurants operating on thin margins, even incremental inefficiencies can have outsized financial consequences. In the Access Hospitality report, it was found that 35 percent reported spending one to two hours a day just switching between systems, and just over 27 percent reported spending 30 to 60 minutes a day. At a strategic level, this introduces a critical consideration for restaurant leaders: technology decisions are no longer just about feature sets, but about how effectively systems work together. articles.title: Allergen Labels Are Changing. Restaurant Operations Need to Keep Up
articles.titleKo: Allergen Labels Are Changing. Restaurant Operations Need to Keep Up
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Ask anyone who’s worked a Saturday lunch rush, the line doesn’t stop and the register can’t be fast enough. Now what happens when a guest asks about an allergen, whoever’s at the counter needs a fast, correct answer. There is no time to pause or asking the guest to “Wait while I check”. It’s true that any disruption can send you into the weeds. What’s new is that two states have now written it into law that a guest not only be told but shown on the container. California’s Allergen Disclosure for Dining Experiences Act has been in effect since July 1 for restaurant chains with 20 or more locations nationwide. It requires the nine major allergens to be disclosed for every menu item, whether a guest is reading a printed menu, a kiosk screen, or an app. New York is coming at it from a different angle: starting November 12, 2026, any food prepared and packaged on-site before a customer orders it, must carry a written allergen notice. Unlike California, this rule in NY applies to all operators no matter the size. Think of the sandwich or salad already sitting in the case, before it was just a price and item name on the tag. Now it has to contain ingredients and display any of the nine major allergens it may contain. California also cleaned up its date labels, standardizing “use by” for safety and “best if used by” for quality, and dropping consumer-facing “sell by” dates altogether. For a single unit operator, meeting any one of these is a matter of getting one menu right. For a chain running the same items across hundreds of units, it’s a different job, and it’s the one I spend most of my time on with our customers. Compliance and speed of service are the same conversation I’ve never liked treating allergen disclosure as a legal item that lives like a secret somewhere. An uninformed staff in a high-volume environment makes this an operations issue, because it has the ability to hold up everything exactly when things are moving fastest. More than 33 million people in the U.S. live with a food allergy, and more of them are checking allergen information before they order than ever did before. When a menu board says one thing and the ingredients say another, that plays out at the counter, in front of a guest, with a line behind them, not on paper somewhere upstream. A fast, correct answer keeps that line moving. A wrong one stops it or worse turns into something a lot more serious than a slow ticket time. Where chains actually lose consistency I’ve walked into enough locations across enough chains to know where this breaks down, and it’s rarely dramatic. It’s a manager working off an allergen chart from last quarter’s menu because that’s still what’s taped to the wall, a regional team that updated the drive-thru board or the in-store kiosk three weeks ago but never touched the online ordering app because that is handled by someone else. Worse is a new hire on a Friday night who’s never seen the current version of anything because nobody handed it to them. Multiply that across a few hundred locations running on different timelines and different levels of manager attention, and you get exactly what these laws are trying to prevent: guests getting different, sometimes wrong, information depending on which store they walked into. The chains that handle this well share one habit. They manage allergen and menu data from a single place, push it out to the app, the kiosk, and the printed menu at the same time, and build the process so it doesn’t depend on one manager remembering to swap out a sign. That kind of consistency comes from how the system is built, and it holds up no matter which manager is running the shift. Don’t sleep on the date-label change California’s date-labeling rule can look like the smaller story next to the allergen laws, but for anyone moving high volumes of fresh, packaged product, it’s a real one.

articles.title: Roy Rogers Adds Kickin’ Chicken with Hot Honey to Menu for Limited Time
articles.titleKo: Roy Rogers Adds Kickin’ Chicken with Hot Honey to Menu for Limited Time
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Roy Rogers Restaurants is turning up the heat with Kickin’ Chicken with Hot Honey, a limited-time offering that brings together crispy, hand-breaded chicken and the sweet heat of hot honey for a bold new take on a Roy Rogers favorite. Available for a limited time at participating Roy Rogers locations, Kickin’ Chicken with Hot Honey gives guests a twist on breakfast with the Kickin’ Chicken Biscuit and a spicy kick to lunch with the Kickin’ Chicken Sandwich. Both offerings start with quality ingredients and real preparation. Roy Rogers uses fresh, never-frozen chicken that is hand-breaded for a crispy, golden exterior and juicy bite. Hot honey adds a craveable balance of sweetness and heat, delivering big flavor without losing what guests love about Roy’s chicken. The flavor doesn’t stop with Kickin’ Chicken. Hot Honey is also joining Roy Rogers’ signature sauce lineup as a dipping sauce, giving guests another way to customize their Roy’s favorites. Whether drizzled over Kickin’ Chicken or paired with another menu favorite, the new sauce builds on Roy Rogers’ longstanding sauce story and commitment to letting guests enjoy their meal their way. “At Roy Rogers, we believe there’s no substitute for doing things the right way, and that starts with the food we serve,” said Jim Plamondon, Co-president. “Kickin’ Chicken takes the quality our guests already know and love and gives it a bold, sweet-and-spicy twist. It’s familiar enough to feel like Roy’s, but with something new that makes you want to come back for another bite.” The Kickin’ Chicken Sandwich pairs Roy Rogers’ crispy chicken with hot honey for a combination of savory, sweet and spicy. For breakfast fans, the Kickin’ Chicken Biscuit brings that same flavor to a warm biscuit for a morning with a little extra kick. The limited-time launch builds on the brand’s longstanding commitment to hearty, freshly prepared food. From its signature roast beef and burgers to its hand-breaded chicken, famous Fixin’s Bar® and signature sauces, Roy Rogers has spent decades giving guests the freedom to enjoy quality food their way. And while Kickin’ Chicken may bring some heat, the idea behind it is classic Roy’s: never frozen, hand-breaded and made with care. You could call it part of the Cowboy Code. Guests can try Kickin’ Chicken with Hot Honey for a limited time at participating Roy Rogers restaurants. Availability and pricing may vary by location. articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Bread Zeppelin , the Dallas-founded fast casual concept known for its signature “Zeppelin,” will open its newest restaurant in Richardson on Wednesday, Sept. 30. Located at 1920 N. Coit Road, Suite 201, the restaurant marks the brand’s 12 th in Texas and continues its growth across the Lone Star State. Opening day kicks off with a ribbon-cutting ceremony alongside the Richardson Chamber of Commerce at 10 a.m. The brand will also host a “bread coring ceremony,” featuring the cutting and coring of the first Zeppelin served at the new restaurant, while The Ticket broadcasts “The Hardline” live from the dining room. Opening day festivities will also include: Free Zeppelins for a year for the first 50 guests* 50% off Entrees from 3 to 7 p.m. at the Richardson location during “The Hardline” live radio remote, in-store only A prize wheel featuring free combos, cookies, drinks, gift cards and loyalty points Mystery receipt giveaways featuring prizes such as a Bread Zeppelin YETI tumbler, earbuds, a Bose speaker and more Opening weekend keeps the fun going with: Free kids meals for children under 10 on Oct. 3 and Oct. 4,* in-store only A QR code giveaway where area organizations and sports teams can enter for the chance to receive sponsorship support from Bread Zeppelin The restaurant will carry the celebration through the following week, Oct. 5-11, with promotions including: Two daily giveaways where guests can scan an in-store code for the chance to win catering for 12 people 25% off entrées after 5 p.m. (limit one entrée per person, in-store only) 25% off catering orders sent to Catering@breadzeppelin.com through Oct. 31 Bounce back offers Bread Zeppelin centers its menu around the Zeppelin, a toasted artisan baguette hollowed out and filled with salads, housemade dressings and proteins prepared fresh daily. Guests can also order any Zeppelin as a bowl, along with soups, seasonal specials and housemade bread pudding created from the bread cores removed from each baguette. Richardson guests can also grab the limited-time Pink Lady through October 31. The seasonal salad features grilled chicken, Pink Lady apples, candied pecans, red onion, goat cheese, Arcadian mix and spinach, all tossed in Champagne Vinaigrette. For each Zeppelin or bowl sold, Bread Zeppelin will donate $1 to Breast Cancer Can Stick It! at DFW restaurants and The Rose in Houston — a Breast Cancer Awareness Month tradition the brand has committed to for the past three years. “Richardson has a real community feel, and the mix of people who work here and families who call the neighborhoods around Coit home is exactly what we look for when considering a new location,” said Co-Founder Troy Charhon. “We want to be the stop on the way home from a Friday night game or the spot somebody grabs before a shift, and you only get that by earning it — one Zeppelin at a time.” Since launching in 2013, Bread Zeppelin has steadily expanded across Texas while maintaining its focus on fresh preparation and guest experience. “The best part of any opening is watching somebody take a first bite of something we’ve been making for thirteen years,” said Co-Founder Andrew Schoellkopf. “We’re bringing the full experience to the community, with everything made to order, dressings made in-house and even bread pudding for those with a sweet tooth. We can’t wait for our new neighbors to experience it with us.” The Richardson restaurant will be open daily from 10:30 a.m. to 9 p.m. For more information or to view the menu, visit breadzeppelin.com or follow @breadzeppelin on social media. *Restrictions apply. articles.title: Denny’s Opens Nominations to Honor 30 Hometown Heroes
articles.titleKo: Denny’s Opens Nominations to Honor 30 Hometown Heroes
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . Today, America’s Diner opened nominations for Denny’s Heroes: A Grand Slam Thank You, a nationwide search for stories of generosity, resilience, leadership, and service that have changed lives or made communities stronger. Every town has a hero who never stops showing up. The teacher who keeps snacks in her desk because she knows which kids come to school hungry. The coach who always finds room for one more child who needs somewhere to belong. The volunteer who keep coming back every Saturday because they know their neighbors are counting on them. If someone immediately came to mind, Denny’s wants to hear their story and celebrate it. Nominations are open now through October 30 at dennysheroes.com. “Every day in our restaurants, we see what it means when someone remembers your name, notices when you need something or makes room for you,” said Chris Bode, president and chief executive officer of Denny’s. “A Grand Slam Thank You carries that same care beyond our doors. Together with our franchise owners, we’ll bring the diner to 30 hometown celebrations honoring individuals who keep showing up for others. Denny’s was built one hometown at a time, and we want to bring communities together to celebrate the people who make those hometowns stronger.” A nomination may recognize one individual. Nominees may include educators, caregivers, first responders, coaches, veterans, volunteers, community supporters or anyone who is always the first to step forward when something needs to be done. From the stories submitted, Denny’s will select 30 heroes to receive a “Grand Slam Thank You,” a Denny’s-catered hometown celebration for up to 50 guests hosted by a local franchise owner. The celebration also looks ahead to an important milestone for America’s Diner. In May 2027, Denny’s will mark 50 years since the Grand Slam was first added to the menu in several Atlanta, Ga restaurants in celebration of baseball legend Hank Aaron. As that anniversary approaches, Denny’s Heroes: A Grand Slam Thank You carries the spirit of an iconic meal created to honor a hometown hero forward by recognizing a new generation of people making a difference in communities across the country. “The people we hope to honor will never call themselves heroes. They are too busy making sure someone is fed, safe, seen or given another chance,” said Fasika Melaku, chief people, enterprise communications and social impact officer of Denny’s. “We’re asking people to stop for a moment and think about someone who has made a difference in their life, their family’s life or their community, and then tell us their story. No one should have to become famous to hear the words, ‘We see you. We see the need you noticed, the care you gave and the people who are stronger because you showed up. What you did mattered.'” Nominate your hero today at dennysheroes.com. The post Denny’s Opens Nominations to Honor 30 Hometown Heroes appeared first on FSR magazine .

articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Love & Honey Fried Chicken, the premium fast-casual concept known for chef-driven fried chicken, heartfelt hospitality, and a growing footprint across the Northeast, is targeting Massachusetts for franchise expansion. Building on its recent entry into Rhode Island with a location in Cranston, Love & Honey is seeking experienced operators to help bring the brand to Massachusetts for the first time. With more than a decade of experience building successful franchise businesses, Playa Bowls franchise owner Amy Lupo has established herself as a dedicated operator, community leader and advocate for the franchise system. After growing Nothing Bundt Cakes from one to seven locations in the Memphis market, she became Playa Bowls’ first franchise owner in Tennessee and has since grown to four shops across the Memphis area. Now, Lupo has been named a 2026 Franchisee of the Year by the International Franchise Association (IFA). “Our shops are part of our communities, and supporting the people and organizations around us has always been important to me,” said Lupo. “From supporting the Memphis Child Advocacy Center through Red Tub Day to creating a special experience for a local Make-A-Wish child at our Collierville shop, some of the most rewarding moments have come from being able to give back to the community that has supported us. Being named an IFA Franchisee of the Year is incredibly meaningful because it recognizes not only the business we’ve built, but the impact we’ve been able to make along the way.” Since opening her flagship East Memphis location in May 2024, Lupo has quickly built momentum for Playa Bowls in the Memphis market. Her shop earned the brand’s Rising Star Award for exceptional first-year performance, driven by strong sales, outstanding guest engagement, positive reviews, and high loyalty program participation. Building on that early success, Lupo opened an additional location in 2025 and two more in 2026. Alongside that growth, Lupo and her team have remained active in the Memphis community. In addition to their work with the Memphis Child Advocacy Center and Make-A-Wish, they also support local sports and cheer teams through sponsorships and team meals. Lupo’s success as a franchise owner is matched by her commitment to strengthening the system around her. As an active member of Playa Bowls’ 2026 Franchise Advisory Council, she brings her operational experience beyond her own shops, participating in local shop marketing pilot programs for new openings and emerging markets, beta-testing new technology and providing feedback to improve processes across the broader network. She also speaks with prospective franchise owners during the discovery process and mentors fellow operators across the system. “Franchisees of the Year demonstrate what franchising is all about – individuals who have committed their lives and careers to the betterment of those around them, building something bigger than themselves,” said Matt Haller, President and CEO of the International Franchise Association. “We are proud to recognize Amy Lupo with IFA’s highest honor for individual franchisees and celebrate her commitment to making a difference both within her business and beyond.” Lupo was honored at the IFA26 Advocacy Summit in Washington, D.C., which took place September 14-16, for excellence in entrepreneurship, community outreach, workforce development, and service to others. The prestigious award recognizes franchise owners who exemplify excellence in their businesses, communities, and franchise systems. As two of East Coast Wings + Grill’s first franchise owners, the Weavers have spent more than two decades demonstrating an unwavering commitment to operational excellence, community leadership, and brand stewardship. As successful multi-unit operators, they have earned numerous company awards for operational performance while building loyal teams and creating restaurants that have become gathering places within their communities. The IFA’s Franchisee of the Year awards recognize franchise owners who demonstrate excellence in business, give back to their communities, create opportunities for those around them and support their fellow franchisees. The Weavers were honored at the IFA26 Advocacy Summit in Washington, D.C., Sept. 14-16, for being an outstanding franchise owner with excellence in entrepreneurship, community outreach, workforce development, and service to others. Nominated by their brand, the IFA Franchisee of the Year awards are given to top franchisees from IFA member brands across industries and communities around the country. “Franchisees of the Year demonstrate what franchising is all about – individuals who have committed their lives and careers to the betterment of those around them, building something bigger than themselves,” said Matt Haller, President and CEO of the International Franchise Association. “Through their leadership, they create jobs and build careers, give back to their communities, and support other franchisees, all while exemplifying the entrepreneurial spirit at the heart of franchising. We are proud to recognize Brent and Sherry Weaver with IFA’s highest honor for individual franchisees and celebrate their commitment to making a difference both within their business and beyond.” What distinguishes the Weavers is their long-term vision. Their newest project in the Piedmont area of North Carolina, goes beyond opening another restaurant. They are developing the property from the ground up to own the real estate and serve as their own landlords while creating a commercial center anchored by East Coast Wings + Grill. At the same time, they are preparing for a generational transition, mentoring their son, Andrew, to eventually lead the family’s restaurants and keep the business family-owned and locally operated for decades to come. Their commitment to community showed following Hurricane Helene in 2024, when the Weavers organized donation drives across all three of their Winston-Salem area restaurants, rallying guests and fellow franchisees and partnering with the franchise support team to deliver food and essential supplies. Through those efforts, thousands of donated items and care packages reached families impacted by the storm. “Brent and Sherry represent the very best of what franchising can be,” said Sam Ballas, CEO and Founder of ECW+G. “They have built an exceptional business, but what stands out just as much is their generosity and their vision for the future. Brent and Sherry embody the spirit of this award, and we could not be prouder to see them recognized by the IFA.” East Coast Wings + Grill continues to seek qualified entrepreneurs interested in building scalable, community-focused full-service restaurants with the support of an established franchise system. articles.title: Inside KFC’s ‘Open House,’ the Restaurant Built to Win America Back
articles.titleKo: Inside KFC’s ‘Open House,’ the Restaurant Built to Win America Back
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . KFC’s Kentucky Fried comeback is coming to life in the U.S. On September 27, the legacy brand will unveil its newest restaurant concept in McKinney, Texas. Dubbed “Open House,” it’s a place to serve guests, experiment with new approaches, and identify what can be scaled across KFC’s 3,500 U.S. units. “KFC is such an iconic brand … there is so much love for it, but it’s almost as if KFC lives in people’s memories and not so much in the moment,” Catherine Tan-Gillespie, president of KFC U.S., says. “With our Open House, we are inviting America to come in and try us again.” The opening is the latest step in a global reset. In June, KFC unveiled its next chapter , a multipoint update built around boneless chicken, sauces, and a refreshed brand identity that includes a new logo and modern restaurant design. Open House is where that vision takes physical form in the U.S. Inspired by the Colonel’s belief everyone was welcome at his table, Open House is as much an innovation hub as it is a signal of where the brand is headed: an upgraded menu with approachable value, modern design, and expanded dayparts, all still rooted in KFC’s heritage, the company says. KFC is corporately going to test the location before phasing in any changes to other stores. Designed to be seen The 3,400-square-foot restaurant draws on midcentury modern design as a nod to the brand’s history. And from the outside, it’s nearly all glass. “The design of the restaurant is atypical … QSRs typically don’t have many oversized windows, but people need to see and trust what’s happening inside,” Tan-Gillespie says. “This is important to get more customers into the restaurant.” Outside, there’s a patio and breezeway, dual drive-thru lanes, and a dedicated mobile pickup zone. Even the drive-thru gets the Open House treatment: Music plays through the lane to set the vibe and make the wait feel less like a transaction and more like part of the experience. Inside, warm timber accents meet pops of KFC’s signature red. The 52-seat dining room feels like someone’s home, with cozy corner booths, flexible seating, and succulents set in white rock, a nod to the Texas landscape. The signature is the store’s “Celebration Booth”—a glass-fronted nook wrapped in digital screens that rotate through themes. At any moment, guests might be surrounded, quite literally, by golden fried chicken. It’s free, requires no reservation, and doubles as regular seating when not in use. There’s also the “Swag Bar,” stocked with exclusive KFC apparel and souvenirs. By putting its iconic merch front and center, the brand gives guests one more reason to linger and spend. Digital where it helps Inside and out, Open House runs on a simple philosophy: “digital where it helps, human where it matters.” Externally, the digital half means self-order kiosks and menuboards. But the bigger bet may be the one guests never see. Luke Jackson, chief operating officer of KFC U.S., calls the back of house an “operations playground,” one where the smartest upgrades aren’t always the flashiest. “When we talk about simplification, we often think about new, big, shiny pieces of equipment,” Jackson says. “Actually, this is just about being ergonomically smart … What do [team members] do first, second, third, without telling them? And then you’re able to design around that.” Take the fry line. In many KFCs, open and pressure fryers sit under separate hoods, and cooks can walk 10 or more paces to get finished chicken to the warmers. At Open House, it’s all under one hood, steps from the warmers. That’s no small thing when chicken, still hand-breaded in-house, is cooked nearly every hour. The breading tables received the same treatment. Instead of running a different flavor on each, both now hit a single flavor, so the crew isn’t juggling two nearly identical flours. articles.title: The Case for Making Quick Service More Experiential
articles.titleKo: The Case for Making Quick Service More Experiential
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . The challenge for QSR today is that it has to go beyond speed and convenience. It’s been a tough few years for QSR chains. Traffic to venues is declining (for example, nearly 40 percent of Americans spend less at restaurants than a year ago ), while operational pressures are multiplying. Spikes in fuel, energy and commodity prices have forced many chains to hike menu prices, steadily turning consumers off . No surprise, then, that an in-person restaurant visit now needs to offer something extra, something delivery or home dining can’t match. Younger generations especially are seeking higher-quality experiences when they go out ( 74 percent of consumers would choose a venue for a more ‘elevated’ experience). This cultural shift is reflected in the growth of competitive socializing venues like Flight Club, F1 Arcade, Level99 and TOCA Social . In the U.K., real estate specialist Savills has tracked a 58 percent increase in competitive socializing venues to 800 since it began measuring the sector in 2018. In the US, the category has grown by 84 percent since 2023, with more than 900 locations now spread across the US and Canada ( White Hutchinson, 2026 ). These venues include QSR offers, but what makes them so popular goes beyond the food and even the activities themselves. It’s about the communities they build, the stories people want to join, the reasons they have to return. They offer a useful playbook for traditional quick service. Finding touchpoints for theatre The lessons here aren’t about handing floorspace to F1 simulators or putting greens — convenience will always drive QSR. The takeaways are more conceptual. They’re about seeing the whole customer journey, imagining the visit as an experience rather than a functional sequence of events. For QSR, that means looking hard at the moments usually treated as operational necessities: the entrance, the queue, the order screen, the wait, the pick-up point. Can each one do more brand-building work? More to engage, delight and stick in the mind. If competitive socializing shows us one thing, it’s that every touchpoint can be treated as theatre. Working with Level99, we knew, for example, that the arrival area had to change—from a one-dimensional sign over the door into an experiential portal. It’s now a spectacularly lit, sensory threshold that builds energy before guests even enter. F1 Arcade does something similar with its grid lighting, pit-lane cues and track-inspired details. In a QSR environment, the same principle could turn dead time into time for brand narrative. Instead of asking customers to stand below a screen waiting for their number to be called, brands could use sound, motion, language and visual storytelling to build anticipation around what is being made, where it comes from and why it matters. A reason to stay QSR can also do far more to design reasons to stay, not just facilitate ordering and collection at speed. If in-person visits now compete with delivery, grocery and eating at home, the physical venue has to offer what those channels cannot: atmosphere, connection and a sense of occasion. For Level99, we designed a central social destination bar that amplified the insight that the venue’s energy comes from its players not its technology. The new ‘Energy Core’ bar has become a place for players to recharge, reconnect and become part of the wider social experience – a piece of immersive storytelling that transforms the space into a meaningful part of the brand narrative. Boda Borg is another good example, as it deepens engagement by feeding visitor preferences and gameplay data back into scores, feedback and final wrap-ups. That makes the experience feel personal and connected, rather than simply using data to push offers. QSR venues could experiment with such different approaches. articles.title: How BJ’s Restaurants is Building a Better Business Over Time
articles.titleKo: How BJ’s Restaurants is Building a Better Business Over Time
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on FSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily FS Insider . BJ’s Restaurants CEO Lyle Tick has observed today’s customer dynamic unfolding through a couple of avenues. If you look at the endless string of data reports on the subject, you’d assume, understandably, the diner was under some degree of stress. He views what’s taking shape differently, however: One, is what Tick refers to as “durable and disposable transactions.” The kind of traffic a brand like BJ’s, and other casual-dining chains, competes for falls under this distinction. Or, “the social splurge space.” “Whether it’s the weekly, a couple of times a month, I’m going out with friends. I’m going out with family. It’s an experience-based thing. And I think people protect those things,” Tick said during the Barclays Annual Global Consumer Staples Conference. “Disposable transactions” are occasions more like weekday lunch or grabbing a quick dinner on the way home. Customers, he said, tend to shed such visits in favor of guarding their social trips. “And so, that’s where we compete,” Tick said. “That’s where we do well. And I think that’s potentially a dynamic why we’re doing well.” It’s a present landscape, he continued, favoring some of BJ’s peers (like Chili’s) where a spread of winners and losers has formed among full-service chains; a time where consumers, when they do decide to open their wallets, are prioritizing a great exchange for their dollars. The brands thriving, Tick said, are those investing in their value proposition holistically. “Their product, their service, their atmosphere, and making sure they have a place where their team members and their guests want to be,” he said. “And those folks are winning more. I think, thankfully, over the past couple of years, we’ve made pretty significant progress across those areas.” This larger macro picture might be fueling BJ’s, but it’s merely a piece of much-larger jigsaw for a brand coming off one of its best periods in years. The chain posted same-store sales growth of 6.5 percent in Q2 as traffic leapt 8.3 percent. It marked BJ’s eighth consecutive run of comps and traffic growth and the loftiest comps bump in three years and highest traffic in four. Mother’s and Father’s Day sales spiked north of 8 and 3 percent, respectively, year-over-year, and more than 80 stores broke daily or weekly records. And regarding Tick’s notion of a pressured consumer, BJ’s didn’t feel it—it notched growth through all geographies, dayparts, and channels. Sales increases were evenly distributed across the week as well. Again, he feels guests are simply doing what they have to so they can socialize and indulge. BJ’s is there to fill that need-state when it arises. And in recent quarters, as Tick, who was named CEO last June after serving as president and chief concept officer (he was formerly brand president of Buffalo Wild Wings from 2018 to 2023), kept sharing industry-fronting results with investors, he was often asked to compartmentalize BJ’s success. Bj’s has been on a sales and traffic run. In other terms, was there one thing driving the surge? That’s a byproduct of life on Wall Street, where analysts value quarter-to-quarter recaps as much as long strips of growth. Tick said, from his view, it doesn’t quite work that way. BJ’s doesn’t have a “one thing” to explain its upturn. Over the past two years, it’s been a combination of foundation-setting plans alongside marketable wins, starting with operations. Pillar fixes showed in guest and employee metrics, Tick said. BJ’s then followed by unlocking “the power of the Pizookie,” building an everyday value platform, improving product—beginning with pizza—and moving through burgers and its chicken sandwich. Also, “putting a fair bit” of money back into facilities and driving BJ’s remodel program. On October 6, 2026, Oak & Stone, the popular craft kitchen and self-pour tap wall restaurant concept, is set to open its newest location in The Villages’ Eastport Town Center, one of the community’s newest developments. The opening is the latest in a series of new location openings and marks Oak & Stone’s entry into Central Florida, bringing the concept’s footprint to 10 locations across Florida and Texas. Located at 7016 Central Lake Drive in the heart of Eastport at The Villages, FL, the 6,049 square foot space features indoor seating for 78, an indoor-outdoor bar, patio seating for 38, and two 12-top fire feature tables. The Tap Wall, a signature element of the Oak & Stone experience, will feature 36 drafts, 16 wine selections, and 14 bourbon selections. “From our made-from-scratch dishes to the self-pour tap wall, Oak & Stone’s bold and inventive approach has attracted the adventurous and the curious,” said Stacy Erickson, Marketing Brand Manager, Oak & Stone. “Our creative takes on everything from our artisan pizzas to our Philly Cheesesteak Egg Rolls are an invitation to The Villages’ community to discover our laid-back tavern atmosphere, explore our elevated classic pub fare, and enjoy the heartfelt hospitality shared by our team.” Oak & Stone is one of the first restaurants to open in Eastport, The Villages. The new lifestyle-driven town center has been designed to inspire gathering and connection and features recreation, golf, parks, shopping and dining experiences, all connected through a network of trails and pathways surrounding Central Lake. Oak & Stone’s look and feel complements the town center’s picturesque, European-influenced design and collection of quaint shops and scaled down buildings that invite casual strolls and distinctive experiences. articles.title: Paris Baguette Announces Halloween Lineup
articles.titleKo: Paris Baguette Announces Halloween Lineup
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . From October 1st through November 1st, guests can choose from donuts and beverages, handcrafted cakes and slices, and specialty donut boxes, perfect for every Halloween moment and celebration. Paris Baguette is turning up the heat this Halloween with a wickedly delicious lineup of sweet-and-spicy treats, alongside seasonal favorites guests love. New this year, the Ghost Pepper Chocolate Marble Mochi Donut puts a fiery twist on rich, indulgent chocolate, while the Ghost Pepper Iced Hot Chocolate brings a cool and spicy spin to the classic cozy favorite. And the Halloween fun doesn’t stop there—fan-favorite cakes, donuts and beverages are back and dressed to impress with ghoulish ghosts, creepy crawlers and gummy worms. It’s a Halloween lineup that’s equal parts spooky, sweet and seriously craveable. Darden Restaurants began fiscal 2027 with sales gains across every segment, led by another strong quarter at LongHorn Steakhouse and a 10 percent same-restaurant sales increase at Yard House. Olive Garden posted a smaller gain, but Darden sees an opportunity to rebuild its weekday lunch business. First-quarter sales rose 5.1 percent to $3.2 billion, supported by 53 net new restaurants and 3.2 percent same-restaurant sales growth. Restaurant-level EBITDA margin held steady at 18.8 percent. The quarter’s sales pattern improved as it progressed, then gained further momentum in September, CFO Raj Vennam said. Lighter portion entrées created a 50-basis-point headwind to the average check. Darden plans to promote the lunch offer in the current quarter and test a new weekday lunch platform with more variety. The work addresses a daypart that has lost ground since the pandemic. Weekday lunch accounts for roughly 20 percent of Olive Garden traffic, and its performance relative to other dayparts is down by hundreds of basis points from pre-pandemic levels. “We’ve seen a little bit more deterioration at lunch than we have in any other place,” CEO Rick Cardenas said during the company’s Q1 earnings call. “We thought it was time, and it was already in our five-year plan to work on lunch.” The brand also sees demand for meals suited to different appetites. Its lighter portion entrées have gained the most traction during weekend lunch, when Olive Garden does not offer a separate lunch menu. Cardenas said guests who order those dishes are visiting more frequently than guests who do not, though the company considers the program a long-term investment. Olive Garden’s Never-Ending Pasta Bowl returned at the start of the second quarter with Spicy Alfredo sauce and Shrimp Fritta among the additions. The brand raised the offer’s starting price after holding it at $13.99 for nearly five years, but kept the unlimited protein add-on at $4.99. Cardenas said early results have exceeded Darden’s expectations, with protein add-ons drawing higher interest than before. All 10,000 Never-Ending Pasta Passes sold immediately after six years off the market. Protein is also influencing Olive Garden’s regular menu development. articles.title: DoorDash Agrees to $131.5 Million Settlement Over Worker Pay
articles.titleKo: DoorDash Agrees to $131.5 Million Settlement Over Worker Pay
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . DoorDash said roughly $6.6 million in payments never reached workers, while another $5.7 million arrived days or, in some cases, weeks late. DoorDash agreed to pay $131.5 million to settle allegations that it underpaid or delayed payments to hundreds of thousands of delivery workers in New York City. The city’s Department of Consumer and Worker Protection described the agreement as the largest worker settlement in New York City history and the largest involving food delivery workers in the U.S. More than $115 million will go to workers, while DoorDash will pay another $16.7 million in civil penalties and costs. The department said its investigation uncovered “systematic violations” of local delivery worker laws. DoorDash, meanwhile, acknowledged that it made mistakes while trying to comply with what it called “the most complex earnings standard for delivery workers in the country.” “Simply put, we screwed up,” the company said in a statement. “Our mistakes meant some Dashers were underpaid or paid late. While these mistakes weren’t intentional, that doesn’t make them okay.” The issues emerged after New York City began enforcing a minimum-pay standard for app-based delivery workers in December 2023. The rate, which is adjusted annually for inflation, currently stands at $22.13 per hour before tips. DoorDash said technical bugs led to errors involving deliveries that crossed city boundaries, included multiple pickup or drop-off points, or were partially completed or canceled. In other cases, the company attributed missed payments to incomplete or inaccurate banking information provided by workers. Approximately 264,000 Dashers will receive a payment under the settlement. That includes about 209,000 workers affected by missing or late payments. DoorDash said roughly $6.6 million in payments never reached workers, while another $5.7 million arrived days or, in some cases, weeks late. The company said less than 1 percent of its payments to New York City Dashers were affected. Workers covered by that portion of the settlement will receive at least $10, even if the original shortage was smaller. A larger share of the settlement stems from a disagreement over how DoorDash calculated compensation for “on-call” time, or the period when a worker was logged into the platform but not actively completing a delivery. City officials said DoorDash excluded several categories of trip and on-call time when determining compensable hours under the minimum-pay rule. DoorDash maintained that workers were paid for on-call time but said its methodology differed from the city’s formula. “We calculated on-call time differently than the City, and believe our approach was fair, practical, and legal,” the company said. “But rather than spend years fighting over whose method was right, we chose to pay Dashers sooner and use the City’s method going forward.” The company will pay more than $83 million to resolve that part of the dispute. The investigation began after dozens of workers reported that DoorDash either failed to pay them or did not pay them on time. The agency subsequently widened its review, analyzing billions of data points covering more than 152 million payment transactions and 110 million working hours. Workers who did not receive timely payments will be compensated at approximately twice the amount they were underpaid, in addition to receiving the original unpaid wages. articles.title: Toastique Adds Raspberry Crumble Smoothie and Cannoli Cloud Coffee

articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Toastique, the vibrant national gourmet toast, juice and coffee bar, is proud to unveil its limited-time menu collaboration with creator, author and lifestyle influencer Kit Keenan. The Kit Keenan x Toastique menu features a creamy Raspberry Crumble Smoothie and rich Cannoli Cloud Coffee, inspired by Toastique’s gourmet offerings and Kit’s favorite recipes from her cookbook, “In Good Taste: Effortless, Chic Recipes for Every Occasion,” debuting in November. “Kit’s Picks” will be available at Toastique locations nationwide from September 25 through November 30, 2026. As wellness increasingly shifts away from restrictive routines and toward everyday choices, consumers are looking for ways to incorporate their favorite ingredients and rituals into the foods and drinks they already love. Toastique and Kit set out to create menu items that balance flavor with thoughtful, high-quality ingredients, demonstrating that wellness doesn’t have to mean sacrificing enjoyment. The Kit’s Picks menu features: Raspberry Crumble Smoothie: A refreshing take on the classic dessert. The Raspberry Crumble Smoothie mirrors a freshly baked berry crisp, made with frozen raspberries, banana, Greek yogurt, vanilla lucuma organic plant protein, oat milk and cinnamon. Packed with 28g of protein, the smoothie is finished with Toastique’s housemade berry jam swirl and gluten-free granola crumble, made without artificial preservatives, for warm notes of cinnamon and caramelized sweetness. Cannoli Cloud Coffee: The decadent flavors of cannoli meet the morning coffee ritual. Available iced, the Cannoli Cloud Coffee features a double shot of espresso and housemade vanilla and almond syrup with a splash of milk. Finished with a rich, housemade cannoli cream cold foam with hints of toasted nuttiness and cinnamon, topped with 60% cacao chocolate and crushed cannoli chips to capture the familiar taste of the Italian dessert while keeping the coffee front and center. “We’re incredibly proud of how this collaboration came together,” said Brianna Keefe, founder of Toastique. “We were able to marry Kit’s distinct culinary point of view with Toastique’s passion for creating dishes that nourish every moment, creating the Raspberry Crumble Smoothie and Cannoli Cloud Coffee completely from scratch. We believe everyone deserves to fuel their bodies without sacrificing flavor, and responsibly sourced, high-quality ingredients should always be on the table.” “Collaborating with Toastique allowed me to bring some of my favorite recipes to life with a wellness-focused spin,” said Kit Keenan. “I love how both drinks capture the flavors I’m most drawn to when I’m craving something delicious. The Raspberry Crumble Smoothie is truly one-of-a-kind, and the Cannoli Cloud Coffee is especially personal to me as it draws inspiration from my Italian heritage. Most importantly, the recipe development process really highlighted our shared goal of making food an enjoyable, approachable part of everyday life. I can’t wait for everyone to get their hands on the new menu and hope they can taste the care and creativity that went into every sip!” To celebrate the launch, Kit is hosting a pop-up at Toastique’s Bryant Park, Manhattan location on Friday, September 25 from 11–12 p.m. ET. New York City residents and visitors can stop by the store, located at 445 5th Avenue, New York, NY 10016, to be the first to sample the Raspberry Crumble Smoothie and Cannoli Cloud Coffee. The first 50 guests will receive a branded Toastique tote bag with the purchase of the Raspberry Crumble Smoothie or Cannoli Cloud Coffee. Guests who purchase one of the new menu items will also be entered into a giveaway to win a copy of Kit’s new cookbook, releasing November 10, 2026. articles.title: PJ’s Coffee Plans New Shop Near its Original Location
articles.titleKo: PJ’s Coffee Plans New Shop Near its Original Location
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . PJ’s Coffee is returning to its roots with a new location at 7700 Maple St., just blocks from where founder Phyllis Jordan opened the brand’s first one — PJ’s Coffee & Tea Co. — in 1978. Located between Carrollton Avenue and Broadway Street, the approximately 1,600-square-foot coffee shop will bring the New Orleans-born brand back to where Jordan first introduced her vision for a neighborhood coffeehouse. The new location will feature a refreshed PJ’s Coffee design, indoor seating and an outdoor patio. While PJ’s Coffee has grown from its original Maple Street shop to nearly 200 locations across the U.S. and internationally, the brand has remained intentional about carrying the character of its New Orleans beginnings into every coffeehouse. Whether a PJ’s is around the corner in New Orleans or thousands of miles away, the goal is to make that first step through the door feel unmistakably PJ’s — from the aroma of 100% Arabica beans greeting guests to the coffeehouse atmosphere inspired by the place where it all began. That connection will be especially meaningful at the new Maple Street location, where the sights, sounds and aromas of a modern PJ’s Coffee will meet a neighborhood deeply connected to the brand. Guests can expect the familiar flavors that have made PJ’s a New Orleans coffee staple for nearly five decades, from hot, iced and frozen coffee beverages to its signature Original Cold Brew, classic beignets, fresh breakfast pastries and other café favorites. “We’re excited to bring PJ’s Coffee back to where it all started,” said Paul, Steven and Scott Ballard, brothers and co-founders of Ballard Brands. “Maple Street means a great deal to the PJ’s Coffee community, and we’re looking forward to being part of the neighborhood again.” The refreshed space will pair those longtime offerings with a contemporary design, creating a neighborhood gathering place that reflects the evolution of PJ’s while honoring the traditions that have connected the brand to New Orleans since Jordan opened the original shop. Jordan’s approach to coffee — centered on high-quality Arabica beans, careful roasting and a passion for the craft — helped establish PJ’s as a fixture of New Orleans coffee culture. Today, that same commitment extends across the brand’s growing footprint, with each location designed to deliver a distinct PJ’s Coffee experience while remaining connected to its New Orleans foundation. To learn more about the New Orleans-born brand, explore the full menu or find a nearby location, visit pjscoffee.com or download the PJ’s Coffee app. The post PJ’s Coffee Plans New Shop Near its Original Location appeared first on QSR Magazine .

articles.title: The Cumberland Backs Hart Hambleton Growth with New Funding
articles.titleKo: The Cumberland Backs Hart Hambleton Growth with New Funding
articles.originalSummary: The Cumberland Building Society has strengthened its support for an established UK country house hotel – along with its fast-growing bakery arm—by providing a refinancing package designed to fuel the next phase of expansion. The society has provided new funding to Hart Hambleton, the Rutland‑based hospitality and food‑and‑drink group behind the business, enabling it to build on its recent momentum and pursue further growth opportunities. Supporting the group’s Hambleton Hall and Hambleton Bakery businesses, the funding builds on The Cumberland’s strong track record in aiding both hospitality organisations and businesses in the food and drinks sector. Owned by Tim Hart, Hart Hambleton has been a part of the region’s hospitality and food and drink offering for more than four decades, attracting guests from across the UK and abroad, as well as holding a strong following of local customers. The group encompasses Hambleton Hall, a Grade II Listed country house hotel, Hambleton Bakery, a food and drink business with eight shops and a cafe, and Hart’s Hotel and Kitchen. Tim established Hambleton Hall in 1980, growing it into a successful business whose restaurant has held a Michelin star since 1982 and regularly features among the top ten country house hotels in the UK, according to The Times and The Telegraph. Alongside the hotel, the Hambleton Bakery has grown into a significant food operation since it was established in 2008, headed up by Julian Carter who worked as a chef in Hambleton Hall. The bakery now manufactures and distributes its own produce, supplying over 200 independent retailers, restaurants and cafes on a wholesale basis, while serving customers directly through its eight owned retail shops and cafe. It has been recognised nationally, being featured in ITV’s Britain’s Best Bakery and Wild About Food in 2012, which is still remembered by visitors today. While successful, Hart Hambleton looked to refinance the hotel and bakery businesses’ lending in a bid to maintain operations while opening up opportunities for future growth. Being introduced to The Cumberland by broker Zain Zaidi of Enness Global, the society’s Commercial team worked to understand the needs of both Hambleton Hall and Hambleton Bakery. As a result, the society’s dedicated Relationship Manager was able to develop a refinancing solution which met the ambition of the group. Tim Hart, Owner of Hart Hambleton, said: “The Cumberland understood what we have built here and what we are trying to achieve. This is not a straightforward business and having a lender with expertise across both hospitality and food and drink sectors made a real difference. “They took the time to understand the group properly, not just the numbers, but the ethos behind what we have built over the years. That level of understanding is increasingly rare, and it gave us confidence from the outset that we were working with the right partner. “The refinancing gives us a strong foundation and the breathing room to focus on what we do best, running exceptional businesses and looking after the people who make them what they are.” With more than 30 years’ experience dedicated to providing commercial lending to hospitality businesses, The Cumberland also supports organisations across the food and drink sector, offering services including commercial mortgages, current accounts and savings accounts. Every commercial mortgage customer is supported by a dedicated Relationship Manager, providing tailored guidance and consistent support throughout the lending process and beyond.

articles.title: Delamere Launches 97ml Oat Drink for Hospotality Industry
articles.titleKo: Delamere Launches 97ml Oat Drink for Hospotality Industry
articles.originalSummary: Delamere has announced the launch of a new 97ml oat drink following the success of its semi-skimmed milk mini bottles in the hospitality and foodservice industries. Designed for hospitality settings, such as hotel room trays, breakfast buffets and on-board catering, the bottles can be used to add to hot drinks or pour over cereal. The oat drink has been developed to offer a plant-based alternative to cows’ milk, enabling accommodation and foodservice providers to cater to different dietary requirements and evolving consumer preferences. The ambient product has a shelf life of up to six months and once opened, it can be treated as fresh milk and stored in the fridge. Each bottle contains 3-4 servings and can be re-closed and stored by guests, eliminating the single-use plastic associated with milk pots and sticks and saving time on repeat deliveries of fresh milk to rooms. The premium glass bottles, capped with an aluminium lid, are fully recyclable, supporting outlets in implementing responsible waste management practices. Available now, the new oat drink can be purchased directly through Brakes and via wholesalers nationwide. Dan Yates, national account manager at Delamere, said: “Our mini milk bottles are already a trusted choice in hotels and hospitality settings, so the creation of a plant-based oat drink in the same format felt like the natural next step when adding to the range. “Sustainable, premium and convenient, we’re confident that it will soon be a staple part of the guest experience.” Located in Knutsford, Cheshire, Delamere has been producing award-winning dairy products for more than 40 years. It supplies an extensive range of speciality goat and cows’ milk based products to retail, wholesale and independent customers across the UK and in over 20 markets around the world.

articles.title: Starbucks to Close 250 North America Locations This Week
articles.titleKo: Starbucks to Close 250 North America Locations This Week
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . Starbucks is on pace to complete 1,500 "uplifts" this year. Starbucks announced Thursday it’s closing about 250 North America locations later this week, or roughly 1 percent of the company’s 18,000-plus store portfolio. Chief operating officer Mike Grams, who was promoted to the role in June 2025 after joining the company from Taco Bell that January, said Starbucks “carefully reviewed” locations and identified restaurants “we do not believe we can consistently deliver the experience we want for customers and partners or where we don’t see a path to acceptable financial performance.” “Closing any coffeehouse is a difficult decision, and we know today’s news will be hard for the partners, customers, and communities affected,” he said in a statement. Starbucks’ North America business has picked up in recent quarters. Same-store sales lifted 8.1 percent in Q3 (6.1 percent two-year stack) after hiking 7.1 percent in Q2 and 4 percent to open fiscal 2026. Comps were flat in Q4 2025 after declining 2 percent in Q3 2025, 1 percent in Q2 2025, and 4 percent in Q1. This flip to green, Grams said, has included faster service, more consistent experience, and “warmer, more welcoming coffeehouses.” It also provided a clearer view of the performance of locations and how some venues continue to underperform despite Starbucks’ efforts. “Every year we close some coffeehouses and open others as part of managing our portfolio,” he said. “And as we shared previously, we remain excited about the significant long-term growth opportunity ahead in North America. We are actively developing a strong pipeline of new coffeehouses and remain committed to growth in North America.” Starbucks said it’s speaking directly with impacted employees and will support them through the transition, including transfer opportunities “wherever possible.” For those unable to be placed in another restaurant, Starbucks noted it would provide severance support. “We’ll also help customers continue their Starbucks routines and connections by directing them to nearby coffeehouses,” Grams added. Starbucks opened 175 net new stores in Q3 globally to exit the period at 41,304. The U.S. comprised 16,933 of those. Overall, Starbucks had 18,371 locations in North America, a 2 percent decline year-over-year from 18,734. So, the company was already taking this rationalization road. Grams said Starbucks has accelerated pace toward completing 1,500 “coffeehouse uplifts.” This past quarter saw the brand surpass 1,000 across North America, reaching its fiscal 2026 goal ahead of schedule. Going back a period, Starbuck finished about 300, meaning more than 650 restaurants were upgraded in Q3 alone. Management hinted 2027 could go even faster. The uplift program prices $150,000 a store and doesn’t result in any time off-line (they happen overnight). The brand developed a refacing initiative where it quickly adds warmth, texture, and better seating at a fraction of the cost of earlier remodels. These also include digital menuboards, which, more broadly, should be in 80 or 90 percent of restaurants by the end of September, allowing Starbucks to better build its afternoon daypart since it can merchandise offerings. Company-operated unit growth in North America is expected to remain modest in 2027, with international shouldering most of the lift. Starbucks in Q3 projected global net store growth of about 1.5 percent this year (compared to 2 percent in 2025), including 600–650 net new locations. After Thursday’s news, global net store growth for fiscal 2026 should come in instead at about 1 percent, with 440 net new stores, reflecting those 250 closures offset by higher net openings overseas. articles.title: Tigermilk Brings Hacienda Grandeur to the Heart of East London
articles.titleKo: Tigermilk Brings Hacienda Grandeur to the Heart of East London
articles.originalSummary: Their modern South American inspired interior brings life to their largest site to dat e Following its successful opening in May, Tigermilk Spitalfields’s interior has emerged as one of the defining elements of the new flagship restaurant by Alexis and Nina Melikov, the group’s largest site to date. Designed by Studio Leche, Tigermilk’s in-house design studio, the space brings together hacienda-inspired architecture, layered materials and a warm, transportive atmosphere that has become central to the guest experience. Conceived as an escape in the heart of Spitalfields, the ambition was to build an environment that guests would immediately want to stay in, rather than one designed purely to be photographed. Central patios, generous proportions, fountains, handcrafted materials and lush greenery give the space its structure and soul, evoking the kind of environment that takes decades to settle into its surroundings. Antique furniture sits alongside bespoke pieces, and reclaimed terracotta, natural stone, marble and aged timber are used throughout, materials that carry history and wear it well. “People rarely talk about specific design features. They talk about the atmosphere,” adds Alexis. “If people leave believing the space possesses a history, then we have succeeded in creating something that feels authentic rather than constructed.” A considered selection of suppliers and craftspeople underpins the interior. Sogni and Pooky provide the lighting, Pierre Frey and Morris the fabrics and upholstery, and Mandarin Stone the marble and stone surfaces. Flexhouse – responsible for custom joinery, millwork and bespoke fabrication – also contributed to the furniture alongside vintage pieces and Leta, while Resources delivered the decorative wall finishes. Together they bring a layered quality to the space, as though each element has its own provenance and story. With its new 280-cover restaurant, hacienda-inspired interiors and striking luminescent bar stocked with more than 2700 bottles, Tigermilk Spitalfields invites guests into what feels like the brand’s thirteenth home. Through a considered interior scheme full of texture and attention to detail, the restaurant offers a transportive South American-inspired experience designed to engage every sense.

articles.title: CAVA Announces Milestone Restaurant No. 500
articles.titleKo: CAVA Announces Milestone Restaurant No. 500
articles.originalSummary: This story was originally published on QSR. To receive daily news and insights, subscribe to our free daily QSR AM Jolt . CAVA announced a significant achievement in the company’s continued national expansion as it commemorates its 500-restaurant footprint. CAVA is currently ahead of schedule and poised to surpass its goal of 1,000 restaurants by 2032. CAVA marked the moment at its Minneapolis restaurant, which opened today at 622 Washington Avenue SE, and ushers in the company’s entrance into Minnesota, bringing its fleet to 30 states and the District of Columbia. Fifteen years after opening its first fast-casual restaurant in 2011, CAVA enters its next chapter with strong new restaurant performance, continued expansion into new markets, and ongoing investment in menu innovation that expands the possibilities of Mediterranean cuisine for guests. “Reaching 500 restaurants is a defining moment for CAVA and a reflection of how far we’ve come,” said Brett Schulman, Co-Founder and CEO of CAVA. “It represents the passion of more than 15,000 CAVA team members, the strength of the brand we have built together, and the deep connection our food and hospitality have created with guests across the country. As we look ahead, we remain focused on thoughtfully scaling CAVA while bringing bold Mediterranean flavors, warm hospitality, and a spirit of generosity to even more communities.” Building the Next 500 CAVAs As CAVA builds toward at least 1,000 restaurants by 2032, it remains focused on staying true to its roots, bringing the same Mediterranean flavors, healthful ingredients, and sense of human connection that have defined the brand from the beginning to every new community it serves. Its development strategy pairs strong restaurant performance with a disciplined approach to entering new markets, building density and investing in the people and infrastructure needed to scale: New restaurants continue to demonstrate strong performance. New restaurant productivity remains above 100%, with new restaurants generating more than $3 million in average annualized sales. CAVA is expanding into new markets while building density in existing ones. CAVA’s development strategy maintains a balanced pipeline across established, in-fill, and greenfield markets in suburban and urban areas. Each restaurant represents months of planning before opening day. From identifying the right real estate to welcoming the first guest, a new CAVA takes months to open and requires coordination across real estate, design, construction, operations, supply chain and training. Extensive preparation helps deliver a consistent CAVA experience from day one. In new markets, approximately 45-50 team members undergo hours of training and preparation, supported by two leads who handle new restaurant openings and 10 station trainers to help ensure guests experience the same high-quality food and warm hospitality in every location. CAVA is building its workforce alongside its footprint. More than 15,000 team members work across CAVA today, with the company expecting to employ more than 30,000 by 2032. Through its Flavor Your Future platform, CAVA creates pathways for team members to build careers and advance into leadership roles, developing the next generation of leaders who will help support the company’s continued growth. “This milestone is the result of years of work building a development engine that can support CAVA’s growth without losing what makes each restaurant special,” said Jeff Gaul, Chief Development Officer of CAVA. “Every opening requires tremendous coordination across teams to identify the right location, design and build the restaurant, and prepare it to become part of a new community. As we look toward our next 500, we’re continuing to strengthen that foundation while staying rooted in the spirit of Mediterranean hospitality – creating restaurants that feel welcoming from day one and are built to serve and connect with their communities for years to come.” 500
